claims.text: Food travels through one long tube: mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and out through the anus.
claims.supporting_quote: The hollow organs that make up the GI tract are the mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and anus.

claims.text: Digestion starts in the mouth, when you chew.
claims.supporting_quote: The digestive process starts in your mouth when you chew.

claims.text: Muscles in the walls of the gut squeeze behind the food and relax in front of it, pushing food along. This is called peristalsis.
claims.supporting_quote: Food moves through your GI tract by a process called peristalsis.

claims.text: The stomach lining makes acid and enzymes that break food down, and the stomach slowly passes the mixed food on to the small intestine.
claims.supporting_quote: Glands in your stomach lining make stomach acid and enzymes that break down food.

claims.text: The small intestine is where most nutrients are taken in: its walls absorb digested food and water into the blood (digested fats go first into lymph vessels).
claims.supporting_quote: The walls of the small intestine absorb water and the digested nutrients into your bloodstream.
supporting_quotes: The lymph system, a network of vessels that carry white blood cells and a fluid called lymph throughout your body to fight infection, absorbs fatty acids and vitamins.

claims.text: The large intestine soaks up water and turns liquid waste into solid stool.
claims.supporting_quote: The large intestine absorbs water and changes the waste from liquid into stool.

claims.text: The liver makes bile, a juice that helps digest fats, and the gallbladder stores the bile between meals.
claims.supporting_quote: Your liver makes a digestive juice called bile that helps digest fats and some vitamins.

claims.text: The liver is the largest organ inside the body; it helps digest food, stores energy, and removes poisons.
claims.supporting_quote: Your liver is the largest organ inside your body. It helps your body digest food, store energy, and remove poisons.

claims.text: The pancreas makes a digestive juice with enzymes that break down carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.
claims.supporting_quote: Your pancreas makes a digestive juice that has enzymes that break down carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.

claims.text: The kidneys filter the blood, taking out wastes and extra water to make urine.
claims.supporting_quote: Healthy kidneys filter about a half cup of blood every minute, removing wastes and extra water to make urine.

claims.text: Each kidney has about a million tiny filters called nephrons.
claims.supporting_quote: Each of your kidneys is made up of about a million filtering units called nephrons.
claims.conflict: NCI SEER (training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/urinary/components/kidney.html) says 'over a million'. 'About a million' fits both; the text calls it a rough size and no item grades the number.

claims.text: Urine flows from the kidneys down two thin tubes called ureters into the bladder.
claims.supporting_quote: The urine flows from the kidneys to the bladder through two thin tubes of muscle called ureters

claims.text: Besides removing waste, the urinary system keeps the body's water level right by changing how much water leaves in urine.
claims.supporting_quote: The urinary system maintains an appropriate fluid volume by regulating the amount of water that is excreted in the urine.

claims.text: The brain and spinal cord make up the central nervous system; the nerves that reach the rest of the body make up the peripheral nervous system.
claims.supporting_quote: The brain and spinal cord are the organs of the central nervous system.

claims.text: Nerve cells, called neurons, do the nervous system's work by carrying signals called nerve impulses.
claims.supporting_quote: Neurons, or nerve cells, carry out the functions of the nervous system by conducting nerve impulses.

claims.text: Sensory neurons carry messages from the senses to the brain and spinal cord; motor neurons carry orders back out to muscles and glands.
claims.supporting_quote: Efferent, or motor, neurons transmit impulses from the CNS to effector organs such as muscles and glands.

claims.text: The cerebrum, the largest part of the brain, controls thinking, learning, emotions, speech, and movements you choose to make.
claims.supporting_quote: The cerebrum controls thinking, learning, problem solving, emotions, speech, reading, writing, and voluntary movement.

claims.text: The cerebellum, at the lower back of the brain, coordinates movement and controls balance and posture.
claims.supporting_quote: It controls movement, balance, and posture.
supporting_quotes: NLM MeSH, Cerebellum (D002531), scope note (https://meshb.nlm.nih.gov/record/ui?ui=D002531): Its function is to coordinate voluntary movements, maintain balance, and learn motor skills.
claims.note: 'coordinates movement' follows MeSH, so the cerebellum is told apart from the cerebrum, which starts the movements you choose to make (c17).

claims.text: The brain stem joins the brain to the spinal cord and controls breathing and heart rate.
claims.supporting_quote: The brain stem controls breathing, heart rate, and the nerves and muscles used to see, hear, walk, talk, and eat.

claims.text: Many reflexes are handled by the spinal cord without waiting for the brain, so you pull your hand off something hot before you even feel the pain.
claims.supporting_quote: For example, with the withdrawal reflex, the reflex action withdraws the affected part before you are aware of the pain.

claims.text: The skull protects the brain, and the bones of the spine (vertebrae) protect the spinal cord.
claims.supporting_quote: The brain is surrounded by the cranium, and the spinal cord is protected by the vertebrae.

claims.text: Hormones are the body's chemical messengers; glands release them into the blood, which carries them to other organs.
claims.supporting_quote: Hormones are your body's chemical messengers. They travel in your bloodstream to tissues or organs.

claims.text: Endocrine glands have no tubes (ducts); they send their hormones straight into the blood.
claims.supporting_quote: The endocrine glands do not have ducts to carry their product to a surface.
claims.conflict: MedlinePlus and SEER group the 'main' glands differently (thymus, parathyroid). A difference of emphasis, not fact; the text says 'some of the main ones, not a full list'.

claims.text: Insulin is a hormone made by the pancreas that helps sugar (glucose) from food get into the body's cells to be used for energy.
claims.supporting_quote: Insulin is a hormone made by the pancreas that helps glucose get into your cells to be used for energy.

claims.text: The pancreas releases insulin when blood sugar is high and a different hormone, glucagon, when blood sugar is low.
claims.supporting_quote: secrete the hormone insulin in response to a high concentration of glucose in the blood

claims.text: The thyroid is a small butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck; its hormones control how the body uses energy.
claims.authority: MedlinePlus (NLM) / HHS Office on Women's Health
claims.supporting_quote: It makes hormones that control the way the body uses energy.

claims.text: There is an adrenal gland near the top of each kidney. It releases adrenaline (epinephrine), especially during stress.
claims.supporting_quote: These two hormones are secreted in response to stimulation by sympathetic nerve, particularly during stressful situations.

claims.text: The skin is the body's largest organ and forms a barrier against germs and injury.
claims.supporting_quote: forming a protective barrier against pathogens and injuries from the environment

claims.text: Sweat glands put sweat onto the skin. As the sweat evaporates (dries), it cools the skin, which helps keep the body from overheating.
claims.supporting_quote: When sweat evaporates, skin temperature is lowered.

claims.text: The outer skin layer (epidermis) is tough and protective;
claims.supporting_quote: The outer layer is called the epidermis; it is a tough protective layer that contains the melanin-producing melanocytes.
claims.note: Only the epidermis description is taken from this page; its sweat-gland location contradicts itself, so the dermis half (c30) uses the NCI Dictionary.

claims.text: the deeper layer (dermis) holds nerve endings, sweat glands, oil glands, and hair roots.
claims.supporting_quote: The inner layer of the two main layers of the skin. The dermis has connective tissue, blood vessels, oil and sweat glands, nerves, hair follicles, and other structures.
claims.note: Re-sourced in the second review: the old source (SEER melanoma anatomy page) put sweat glands in the dermis in one place and in the epidermis in its Sweat Gland entry, so it was dropped for this half of the sentence.

claims.text: Healthy kidneys filter about half a cup of blood every minute.
claims.supporting_quote: Healthy kidneys filter about a half cup of blood every minute, removing wastes and extra water to make urine.

claims.text: Unfiltered blood flows into each kidney through the renal artery, and filtered blood leaves through the renal vein.
claims.supporting_quote: Unfiltered blood flows into your kidneys through the renal artery and filtered blood exits through your renal vein.

claims.text: The bladder stores urine.
claims.supporting_quote: Your bladder stores urine.

claims.text: Oil glands in the dermis put an oily substance onto each hair that keeps it from becoming brittle.
claims.supporting_quote: Sebaceous glands are small, sack-shaped glands which release an oily substance onto the hair follicle that coats and protects the hair shaft from becoming brittle. These glands are located in the dermis.

claims.text: Each hair sits in a hair follicle, a tube-shaped sheath that surrounds and feeds the part of the hair under the skin.
claims.supporting_quote: The hair follicle is a tube-shaped sheath that surrounds the part of the hair that is under the skin and nourishes the hair.

claims.text: A tiny muscle joins each follicle to the skin; when it tightens, the hair stands up and a goosebump forms.
claims.supporting_quote: The arrector pili muscle is a tiny muscle connected to each hair follicle and the skin. When it contracts it causes the hair to stand erect, and a "goosebump" forms on the skin.
